children.value: The latent-state model describes each participant by six parameters, and, given these parameters and the sequence of cues and attacks the participant saw, it implies on every trial a belief about which of the two latent states is active. This chapter uses this belief as a trial-by-trial measure of the uncertainty that the fitted model attributes to the participant, and asks whether the participant’s behaviour follows it in two respects that are not used to estimate the parameters (placement duration) or only in summarized form (net spread, nets on both directions), and whether it is associated with the questionnaire scores.
Measure and models
For each participant, the fitted model was replayed on the participant’s own trial sequence with 200 draws from the posterior of the parameters (
belief_trace_replay.py

). The state uncertainty on a trial is 1 − |2z − 1|, where z is the probability the model assigns to one of the two latent states before the placement of that trial, averaged over the draws; it is 0 when the model is certain which state is active and 1 when both states are equally probable. On the trial after an event (t+1), it therefore reflects the displaced attack of the event trial. The uncertainty was split into the participant’s mean over the session (between-participant component, standardized across participants) and the deviation of each trial from this mean (within-participant component, in SD of the deviations). The replay was computed for all 86 participants, including the nine assigned another model in the model comparison.
U1 to U3, uncertainty and behaviour
tambi_uncertainty_behaviour.R

). Linear mixed models of the log placement duration (U1; sensitivity models with the number of positions used and the shift of the allocation centre as covariates, and without time-outs) and of the net entropy (U2) on both components, condition and trial index, with by-participant random intercepts and slopes for the within-participant component; a binomial mixed model of nets on both directions at t+1 and t+2 after events (U3; strategy class of the previous chapter) on both components, event type, trial and condition, with by-participant random intercepts. The net entropy enters the estimation of the parameters through its mean and SD over the session, so that U2 checks the consistency of the replay rather than providing independent evidence.
Q1, mean uncertainty and questionnaires
tambi_uncertainty_questionnaire.R

). Linear regressions of the participant’s mean uncertainty (over all trials, over stable regular trials and over the placements at t+1 after events; standardized) on the questionnaire and condition (across-condition form) and on their interaction (moderation form), with heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC3) standard errors, in all participants and in those assigned the latent-state model, and with the six parameters as additional covariates. A regression on the six parameters and condition shows which parameters determine the mean uncertainty.
Q2, uncertainty around events and questionnaires.

A linear mixed model of the trial-level uncertainty on position (regular trial, t0, t+1 and t+2 after transitions and after oddballs) × questionnaire, condition and trial index, with by-participant random intercepts, with tests of the questionnaire terms also with cluster-robust (CR2) standard errors, and participant-level regressions of the mean uncertainty at each position as a check.
Q3 and Q4, coupling with behaviour by questionnaire.

The questionnaire forms of U1 and U2 (within-participant component × questionnaire), the corresponding form of U3, and the models of nets on both directions at t+1 and t+2 on the questionnaire with and without the two uncertainty components.
The replayed uncertainty around events

On regular trials, the mean replayed uncertainty was 0.28 in None, 0.23 in Partial and 0.14 in Full. It was lowest on the event trials (0.08 to 0.22) and highest on the first placement after an event, after transitions (None 0.49, Partial 0.53, Full 0.54) and after oddballs (None 0.39, Partial 0.35, Full 0.38). On the second placement, it remained high after transitions in None and Partial (0.40 and 0.43) and was lower in Full (0.24), and after oddballs it was 0.27, 0.21 and 0.15. In the model, the ambiguity of a single displaced attack at t+1 is thus of similar size in all conditions, and the conditions differ in how far it is resolved by the following attack.

The participant’s mean uncertainty was almost entirely determined by the parameters (linear regression on the six standardized parameters and condition, R² = .96). It was higher with higher belief momentum (0.79 SD per SD) and switch probability (0.35) and lower with higher cue sensitivity (−0.22) and placement noise (−0.09, HC3 p = .020); precision weighting and noise reactivity did not contribute (both p ≥ .91). The mean uncertainty at t+1 after events was determined less completely (R² = .57) and depended also on noise reactivity (−0.36), besides belief momentum (0.57) and the switch probability (0.46).
Uncertainty and behaviour

On trials on which the replayed uncertainty was higher than the participant’s own mean, the placement took significantly longer (within-participant component = 0.022 log units per SD, about 2.2 %, SE = 0.002, t(79) = 9.85, p < .001). The association was about half as large and remained significant with the number of positions used and the shift of the allocation centre as covariates (0.010, SE = 0.002, t(81) = 4.92, p < .001) and without time-outs (0.013, p < .001). Participants with a higher mean uncertainty did not place the nets significantly more slowly (between-participant component = 0.023, p = .16), and the conditions did not differ (both planned contrasts p ≥ .17) (
Figure 1

The net entropy was significantly higher on trials with higher uncertainty than the participant’s mean (0.020 bits per SD, SE = 0.007, t(76) = 2.88, p = .005) and in participants with a higher mean uncertainty (0.14 bits per SD, SE = 0.036, t(86) = 3.94, p < .001). Nets on both directions at t+1 and t+2 after events were significantly more frequent on placements with higher uncertainty than the participant’s mean (0.18 log-odds per SD, SE = 0.062, z = 2.94, p = .003) and in participants with a higher mean uncertainty (0.52, SE = 0.184, z = 2.81, p = .005).

The replayed belief about the active state therefore predicted, within participants, how long the placement took and whether the nets were distributed across both directions, and, between participants, how widely the nets were spread and how often they were placed on both directions.
Uncertainty and questionnaire scores

The participant’s mean replayed uncertainty was not significantly associated with any questionnaire in the across-condition form (all participants, slopes between −0.03 and 0.10 SD per SD, all p ≥ .34, all q ≥ .80; participants assigned the latent-state model, STICSA state anxiety 0.17, p = .067, HC3 p = .10, q = .33, all others p ≥ .42), and the same held for the mean uncertainty on regular trials (all q ≥ .49) (
Figure 2

). In the moderation form, the association with OCI depended on condition in all participants (condition × OCI F(2, 78) = 4.12, p = .020, q = .10), with a positive slope in Full relative to None and Partial (0.53, p = .026; HC3 p = .11); within conditions, the Spearman correlations of OCI with the mean uncertainty were .12 (None), −.26 (Partial) and .30 (Full) (all p ≥ .14). In the participants assigned the latent-state model, no condition × questionnaire term was significant (all p ≥ .19). With the six parameters as covariates, all questionnaire slopes were close to zero (between −0.03 and −0.01, all p ≥ .19). The mean uncertainty at t+1 after events was associated with higher STICSA state anxiety in the participants assigned the latent-state model (0.23, p = .042, HC3 p = .012, q = .21, HC3 q = .062), but not in all participants (0.13, p = .24).

Mean replayed state uncertainty over the session against the five questionnaire scores, by condition (one point per participant; lines are least-squares fits within condition).

Around events, the trial-level model showed that the questionnaire slope of the uncertainty differed between positions for OCI (position × OCI F(6, 15021) = 5.00, p < .001, q < .001) and, without surviving the correction, for STICSA state anxiety (F(6, 15021) = 2.50, p = .020, q = .051). The slopes were positive at t+2 after transitions for OCI (0.044 uncertainty units per SD, SE = 0.019, t(116) = 2.34, p = .021) and STICSA state anxiety (0.040, SE = 0.019, t(116) = 2.14, p = .035), and close to zero at the other positions (
Figure 3

); at t+2, the slope after transitions exceeded the slope after oddballs for OCI (0.044, p < .001, q < .001), STICSA state (0.033, p = .001, q = .003) and trait anxiety (0.026, p = .008, q = .014) and BDI (0.022, p = .026, q = .032). With cluster-robust standard errors, however, the position × questionnaire term was not significant for any questionnaire (all p ≥ .33), because the model tests a participant-level score against the variation between trials and events. In the participant-level check, the difference between the mean uncertainty at t+2 after transitions and after oddballs increased with OCI (0.23 SD per SD, HC3 p = .027, q = .13), with the same sign and without significance for the other questionnaires (0.06 to 0.16, all p ≥ .18).

children.alt: Questionnaire slopes of the replayed state uncertainty at each position relative to events (trial-level linear mixed model with random intercepts; estimates and 95 % CI, uncertainty units per SD of the questionnaire). The confidence intervals do not reflect the cluster-robust tests, under which no position × questionnaire term was significant.

Coupling of uncertainty and behaviour by questionnaire score

children.label: Coupling of uncertainty and behaviour by questionnaire score

children.value: The association of the within-participant uncertainty with the placement duration did not depend on any questionnaire (within-participant component × questionnaire, all p ≥ .60), nor did its association with the net entropy (all p ≥ .51) or with nets on both directions after events (all p ≥ .09, all q ≥ .32). Participants with higher and lower questionnaire scores thus took longer and distributed their nets more when the model’s belief was more uncertain, to the same degree.

In the model of nets on both directions at t+1 and t+2 after events, higher STICSA state anxiety (0.46 log-odds per SD, p = .006) and BDI scores (0.37, p = .029) were associated with more placements on both directions. With the within- and between-participant uncertainty in the model, these coefficients were essentially unchanged (STICSA state 0.42, p = .012; BDI 0.38, p = .024), while the between-participant uncertainty retained its own association (0.50 to 0.56 log-odds per SD in all five models). The same held for STICSA trait anxiety (0.30 without and 0.31 with the uncertainty), OCI (0.24 and 0.19) and IU (0.12 and 0.09).

The replayed uncertainty and the questionnaire scores were therefore separate predictors of placing nets on both directions after an event. The more frequent placements on both directions of participants with higher state anxiety and depression scores did not arise from a more uncertain belief about the active state, as the fitted model reconstructs it, but occurred at the same level of that belief.
